content.text:
**Yes—in the current source, `runregression run -j N check` runs up to N independent tests concurrently and starts another whenever one finishes.** It does not wait for all N tests to finish before starting more.

The implementation uses a shell worker pool:

- Each test runs in a separate background process, with its own working directory and output file.
- A FIFO carries completion tokens back to the scheduler, allowing it to refill available slots immediately.
- Lua receives completion events and processes results as tests finish.

See [the worker-pool implementation](/home/maxwell-rosen/gkeyll/gkeyll/lua/Tool/runregression.lua:1234).

A few distinctions matter:

- **Compilation and execution are separate phases.** C tests compile with up to N workers; execution starts after compilation finishes.
- **`-j N` parallelizes different tests**, rather than dividing each simulation across N processes.
- **`--parallel` selects MPI tests.** Those run one MPI collective at a time, even with `-j N`.
- **GPU tests share available devices**; `-j` does not assign a dedicated GPU to each test.

So asynchronous scheduling between tests is already implemented. For example, with `-j 4`, a fifth test starts as soon as any of the first four finishes.

The overall command still waits until everything completes. If you mean returning your terminal prompt immediately, background it:

```sh
gkeyll runregression run -j 4 check > regression.log 2>&1 &
```

This describes the current repository source; an older installed copy could differ. There is also disabled legacy code in this file that used fixed batches, which may explain conflicting impressions.

content.text:
**`test_costs` is optional for concurrency, but useful for minimizing total runtime.** The worker pool keeps up to `-j N` tests running while tests remain queued. Ordering determines how much idle time you get near the end.

Currently, [the sorter runs shortest tests first](/home/maxwell-rosen/gkeyll/gkeyll/lua/Tool/runregression.lua:1962). That gives quick results, but can leave a long test running alone at the end.

For example, with two workers and test durations of 1, 1, 1, and 10 minutes:

| Ordering | Total runtime |
|---|---:|
| Shortest first | 11 minutes |
| Longest first | 10 minutes |

**For your objective, I recommend keeping the costs and scheduling longest tests first.** This generally reduces the idle tail, although estimated durations cannot guarantee an optimal schedule.

Two details in the current implementation also matter:

- The file’s physical ordering is irrelevant: costs are loaded into a lookup table, then tests are sorted.
- Measured costs are saved to a separate per-run file, but subsequent runs still load the source-tree baseline. Scheduling estimates therefore do **not** automatically refresh.

The existing pool already refills workers dynamically. Changing to longest-first scheduling is the straightforward improvement; overlapping compilation and execution would be a separate improvement because those currently have a phase barrier.

I'm inclined to remove the ordering because it creates another piece of infrastructure to maintain. If this will only yield a performance hit in the final regression test, remove the usage of a test_costs ordering. Do asynchronous execution of the regression tests, including this in the CI

I’ll remove cost-based scheduling and keep the worker pool filling slots as tests finish. I’ll also check the CI invocation so it uses concurrent execution. The tradeoff is a potentially longer tail involving the last few tests, rather than necessarily only the final test.
